newsitem.title: USA: Hearing held for Malcolm X grandson.
newsitem.headline: Hearing held for Malcolm X grandson.

text.p: The grandson of Malcolm X, who admitted setting a fire that killed his grandmother, had an long, unusual interest in fires and fantasized about a cartoon character called "Sinister Torch," a child psychologist testified on Tuesday.
At a Family Court hearing to determine what will happen to 12-year-old Malcolm Shabazz, Dr. Elizabeth Osborn described him as having "psychotic systems and delusional thinking."
The boy pleaded guilty earlier this month to setting the fire that killed his grandmother Betty Shabazz.
The 63-year-old widow of slain civil rights leader Malcolm X died on June 23 from burns she suffered on more than 80 percent of her body in a June 1 blaze at her apartment.
Joseph DeCarlo, a state probation officer, testified that Malcolm Shabazz had been the victim of repeated physical and alcohol abuse.

He did not say who inflicted the abuse but said the boy often acted violently toward his mother Qubilah Shabazz. She is one of six daughters of Betty Shabazz and Malcolm X, who was assassinated at the Audobon Ballroom in Harlem in 1965.
He said the boy bears scars on his face, arms and head.
Osborn, a child psychologist and expert in juvenile fire setters, said Malcolm Shabazz apparently set fire to pair of sneakers in the middle of night when he was 3 years old.
She said she met with him earlier this month and reviewed records from his four-month stay at a New York City children's hospital when he was nine.
"Malcolm has a long-standing interest in the subject of fire that reaches unusual proportions," Osborn said. "He had fantasies of setting fires by gasoline."
The boy also created a fantasy "Sinister Torch" character, which he dreamed up from three cartoon characters, she said.
"He held the belief that he was such a character at times," she said. "At other times the character remained a friend."
Shabazz has not been sentenced for setting the fatal fire. He faces a possible term of 18 months in a juvenile detention facility but the term can be extended until he is 18 years old.

Authorities and his attorneys are trying to determine where he should be sent and what kind of treatment he needs. Shabazz did not attend the hearing but came into the courtroom afterward to hug his mother.
Further testimony is scheduled at another hearing before Family Court Judge Howard Spitz on Aug. 8.
